# Story 53 — CHANNELS-1-API: public intake raises tickets through the same service the desk uses (Story: CRM-118)

## Prerequisites

- `TICKETS-1-API` completed: `ticketsService.raise(actor, input)` exists at `api/src/features/tickets/tickets.service.js:73` and is the only path that inserts a ticket, starts SLA clocks and writes the `ticket.create` audit row.
- `CUSTOMERS-5-API` completed: identity resolution by email lives on the customers service (see `api/src/features/customers/resolve.test.js`). This story calls it — it does not build it.
- Coordinate with owners of any other sprint‑5 migration: the next filename in `api/src/platform/db/migrations/` after `0008__tickets_resolution_note.sql` is claimed by whichever story lands first. Rebase and renumber if a `0009__…sql` appears before merge.
- Read `.squad/plan-lessons.md` end‑to‑end before starting; a repeated defect fails review.

## Story Goal

Add a public, unauthenticated intake endpoint that lets an outside caller submit a ticket. The endpoint:

1. Resolves (or creates) the customer from the submitted email via the customers service (CUSTOMERS-5-API), then
2. Raises the ticket through the **same** `ticketsService.raise(actor, input)` the desk uses — no second insert path — with `actor = null` so the audit row records the system as the actor, and
3. Records the arriving channel on the ticket row and on the `ticket.create` audit event (BR-2), and
4. Refuses malformed input with a 422 in the shared `E-1` shape, and
5. Returns a `new`, unassigned ticket (identical to any desk‑raised ticket).

Explicitly **not** in scope:
- The web portal that posts to this route (`PORTAL-1-WEB / CRM-121`).
- Throttling of the intake (`CHANNELS-3-API / CRM-120`).
- Any second channel implementation (`CHANNELS-2-API / CRM-119`).
- Any outbound message (nothing sends email).
- Any `web/` change.

## Product rules (from story)

- **SC-2** — every rule enforced in the API. The intake enforces nothing that the tickets service doesn't already enforce; it delegates.
- **BR-2** — every write leaves an audit row. Ticket creation via intake records `channel: '<channel-key>'` in the audit `after` payload and on the ticket row.
- **E-1** — refusal envelope shared across every route.

Current behaviour: only the authenticated `POST /tickets` raises tickets, `req.subject` is always a signed‑in user, `tickets.channel` does not exist.
New behaviour: a second route, `POST /intake/<channel>/tickets` (see naming decision below), unauthenticated, resolves the customer from the email and raises via the same service; `tickets.channel` is populated on every ticket (existing rows via migration default).

Create the feature directory. Mirror the shape of `api/src/features/customers/`:

- `channels.service.js` — thin orchestration: resolve customer, call `tickets.raise(null, …)`.

`verify-architecture.mjs` will fail the build if any of these import a sibling feature's non‑index file.

#### 1.1 `Create file: api/src/features/channels/index.js`

```js
// The only way into this feature from outside it.
export { channelsRouter } from './channels.routes.js';
export { createChannelsService, KNOWN_CHANNELS } from './channels.service.js';
```

#### 1.2 `Create file: api/src/features/channels/channels.rules.js`

Two exports:

- `KNOWN_CHANNELS` — frozen array of channel keys this story ships. Start with a single value, e.g. `['web']`, keyed to the portal that will call it. A second channel is `CHANNELS-2-API`'s job.
- `validateIntake(input)` — checks the intake‑only fields (email present and syntactically plausible; channel key present and in `KNOWN_CHANNELS`). Returns an array of field names in the same shape `validateRaisedTicket` uses so `unprocessable(fields)` can consume both merged arrays.

Do **not** duplicate subject/body/priority/category validation — those belong to `validateRaisedTicket` in `tickets.rules.js` and the tickets service will run them.

#### 1.3 `Create file: api/src/features/channels/channels.service.js`

```js
import { unprocessable } from '../../platform/http/errors.js';
import { KNOWN_CHANNELS, validateIntake } from './channels.rules.js';

export { KNOWN_CHANNELS };

export function createChannelsService({ customers, tickets }) {
  return {
    // No `actor` argument by design. The intake is unauthenticated; the audit
    // row records the system as actor because `tickets.raise(null, …)` and
    // `audit.record(null, …)` both write `actor?.id ?? null`. An absent actor
    // is an answer, not a gap.
    submit({ channel, email, subject, body, priority, categoryId }) {
      const invalid = validateIntake({ channel, email });
      if (invalid.length > 0) throw unprocessable(invalid);

      // CUSTOMERS-5-API owns identity resolution by email. Channels does not
      // read or write customers directly — it goes through the customers
      // service's index-exported method.
      const customer = customers.resolveByEmail({ email });

      // Raise via the same method the desk uses. Any validation the tickets
      // feature owns (subject/body/priority/categoryId) is enforced here.
      return tickets.raise(null, {
        customerId: customer.id,
        subject,
        body,
        priority,
        categoryId,
        channel, // carried onto tickets.channel and into the audit after-image
      });
    },
  };
}
```

The exact resolver method name must match what `api/src/features/customers/index.js` exports (grep during implementation). If CUSTOMERS-5-API named it differently (e.g. `resolveOrCreate`), use that name and add a one‑line comment referencing the story.

#### 1.4 `Create file: api/src/features/channels/channels.routes.js`

```js
import express from 'express';

import { createChannelsService } from './channels.service.js';

// The intake is deliberately public. `requireSubject()` is what every other
// route places before its handler (api/src/platform/http/permission.js); this
// one places nothing, so `req.subject` is null and the ticket's audit row is
// authored by the system. See CHANNELS-1-API acceptance list.
export function channelsRouter({ customers, tickets }) {
  const service = createChannelsService({ customers, tickets });
  const router = express.Router();

  router.post('/intake/:channel/tickets', (req, res) => {
    res.status(201).json(
      service.submit({
        channel: req.params.channel,
        email: req.body?.email,
        subject: req.body?.subject,
        body: req.body?.body,
        priority: req.body?.priority,
        categoryId: req.body?.categoryId,
      }),
    );
  });

  return router;
}
```

No `requireSubject()`. No `req.subject`. No new middleware.

## Edge Cases & Failure Modes

- **Missing email** — `validateIntake` returns `['email']`; route responds 422 in the shared E-1 shape. Enforced in `channels.service.js` before touching customers or tickets.
- **Malformed email** — same 422 path, field name `'email'`. Do not attempt to normalise beyond trimming; identity resolution owns the semantics.
- **Unknown channel key in the URL** — `validateIntake` returns `['channel']`; 422. Reject rather than 404 so refusals stay in one shape (E-1). If the product prefers 404 for the path segment, keep behaviour consistent with how the tickets router treats unknown `id`s and add a note in the test.
- **Missing ticket fields (subject/body)** — `tickets.raise` throws `unprocessable([...])` naming the fields. The channels service does not swallow it; the route returns 422.
- **Unknown `categoryId`** — `raise` throws `unprocessable(['categoryId'])` (see `tickets.service.js:108–109`). Intake behaviour identical to desk.
- **Customer resolution creates a new row** — the audit row for the customer create is written by the customers service, actor `null` (system). Do **not** write a second customer‑create audit row from channels.
- **Concurrent intakes for the same new email** — customers service owns uniqueness on email (see `api/src/platform/db/customers_email.test.js`). Any conflict surfaces as a `ConflictError`; the intake propagates it unchanged.
- **`req.subject` is not null despite public route** — regression: assert in the test that a request with a stale/invalid `Authorization` header still lands with `actor = null` in the audit row.
- **Bypass attempt** — direct `insertTicket` from channels would skip SLA clocks and audit. The guarantee test (see Test Plan #3) proves the intake path cannot ship a ticket without the audit row.
- **Half‑applied migration** — `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL DEFAULT 'desk'` is safe on SQLite; back‑filled rows read as `'desk'`. Rollback is a `DROP` (see Migration / Rollback).
- **OpenAPI drift** — if `channel` is added to the schema but not to `publicShape`, the contract test fails. Add both in the same commit.
- **`verify-architecture.mjs` violation** — importing `../tickets/tickets.service.js` directly from `channels/` is forbidden; the plan routes everything through `../tickets/index.js` and `../customers/index.js`.

## Migration / Rollback

- **Forward:** running `migrate.js` applies `0009__tickets_channel.sql`. Existing rows get `channel = 'desk'` via the column default.
- **Rollback:** SQLite has no `DROP COLUMN` before 3.35, but the CI SQLite is modern; if a rollback is required, ship `0010__tickets_channel_rollback.sql` with `ALTER TABLE tickets DROP COLUMN channel;`. Prefer a forward fix.
- **Half‑applied state:** if the migration ran but the code deploy failed, existing routes keep working — `insertTicket` without `channel` writes the default; `publicShape` without `row.channel` selection returns `undefined`, which fails the contract test in CI. Roll forward.

## Review note — what this plan got wrong

Five corrections, four of them in code the plan wrote out in full.

1. **`customers.resolveByEmail({ email })` takes two arguments, not one.** The
   real signature is `resolveByEmail(actor, input)`. Called the plan's way, the
   object lands in `actor` and `input` is `undefined`, so every single request
   is refused 422 naming `email` — the intake would never have worked once. The
   plan also hedged about it ("grep during implementation; if CUSTOMERS-5-API
   named it differently, use that name"), which is the tell L-50 names: a plan
   that hedges is a plan that did not look. The method had been merged an hour
   earlier and is nine lines from the file the plan told the executor to read.

2. **The tickets feature may not know the channel list.** Task 3.4 had
   `tickets.rules.js` validating a channel as "in `KNOWN_CHANNELS` or the
   sentinel `'desk'`" — and `KNOWN_CHANNELS` lives in the channels feature, so
   that is one feature importing a sibling's internals, which
   `verify-architecture.mjs` fails on every push. Tickets now stores what it is
   given and defaults to `'desk'`; which names are valid is the channels
   feature's rule, checked before it calls.

3. **A malformed ticket would have left a customer behind.** The plan validated
   the channel and the email in the intake and left the ticket's own fields to
   `tickets.raise` — which runs *after* the customer has been resolved, and
   resolution creates one when the address is new. A public form is exactly
   where malformed requests come from, so every rejected submission would have
   added a customer row and nothing else.

   Fixing it properly needed the tickets feature's own rule at a moment when
   there is no `customerId` to check yet. `validateRaisedTicket` was split:
   `validateTicketFields` holds the subject/body/priority/category rules and is
   exported through the feature's index, and `validateRaisedTicket` is now that
   plus the customerId check. One rule in one place. The alternatives were a
   second copy of the rules in channels, or passing a placeholder id to a
   validator whose job is to refuse placeholders.

4. **An unknown channel is 404, not 422.** The channel is a path segment, and a
   422 names a field in a body the caller sent — there is no such field. 404 is
   also what CHANNELS-2-API will keep for a name nothing has ever heard of,
   while splitting off 501 for the three the brief names and has decided
   against.

5. **"Either is fine" was not.** On two customers-service instances the plan
   said "the instances are stateless around `db`, so either is fine". They are,
   today. `compose.js` now builds one and hands it to both routers, and
   `customersRouter` takes the service instead of building its own — one
   instance means one answer to what the customers service is, and "harmless
   today" is the kind of harmless that stops being harmless with nobody
   noticing.

What the plan got right and is worth keeping: the route shape
`POST /intake/:channel/tickets`, with the channel as a path parameter, which
gives CHANNELS-2-API's 501/404 distinction a natural home; the `NOT NULL
DEFAULT 'desk'` column, so every row that existed before the intake is valid
and honest; and putting the channel on the audit row as well as the column.

### On the two test files the plan named and this story did not create

`channels.rules.test.js` — `isImplemented` is membership in a one-entry frozen
list. `intake.test.js` drives it through the route for three names, which is the
behaviour; a unit test beside it would be testing `Array.prototype.includes`.
When CHANNELS-2-API gives the list a second dimension — known-and-decided-
against, against never-heard-of — the rule gets a shape worth testing on its
own, and that story can add the file.

`channels.guarantee.test.js` — the criterion it was for ("bypassing the service
must fail a test") is proved inside `intake.test.js` instead, and it was nearly
proved by assertions that do not. `allowedTransitions` is derived from the
status at read time, `revision` is defaulted by the column, and being in the
queue only means a row exists: all three are true of a ticket inserted around
the service, so a test asserting them proves nothing it claims. The service-
level clocks are the difference — S-1 starts both from the ticket's creation
and only `tickets.raise` writes them. An intake rewritten to insert its own row,
returning a shape indistinguishable from the real one, reddens three tests. That
was run, not assumed.
